title: Make Teaching the Job You Want It to Be. Be Yourself, Express Yourself and Have Fun With It! -yourself-and-have-fun-with-it/
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington, best known for his advocacy of precise teaching technique and assertive behaviour management, uses this post to argue that technical rigor and personal enjoyment are not in tension -- sustaining a 30-year career across six schools required him to genuinely enjoy the job, not just execute routines. He organizes his advice around four personal domains: building rapport through taking students seriously rather than through mere friendliness; making deliberate curriculum choices within an over-stuffed syllabus that keep the teacher inspired; developing student agency by training students to lead their own learning rather than defaulting to teacher-delivered notes; and sustaining a driven sense of mission that pushes follow-through on homework, practicals, and hard thinking. Throughout, Sherrington pushes back against critics who dismiss him as an out-of-touch consultant, pointing to his own maxed-out timetables and continued teaching of examination classes even as a headteacher. The piece closes as direct advice to new or jaded teachers: find your own version of enjoying the job, since a teacher's authentic energy is what makes both the teaching and the learning work.
points: Sherrington argues that technical precision in teaching and genuine personal enjoyment of the job are not opposed -- sustaining a long career depends on doing the job in a way that is authentically yours.

He identifies teacher confidence, not curriculum design, as the real bottleneck for student agency: a "vicious circle of teacher doubt" is what most often prevents students from being trusted to lead their own learning.

Even within an "over-stuffed" UK curriculum, Sherrington insists there remain constant small choices -- the poem, the example, the demo -- that let a teacher stay personally inspired rather than merely delivering content.

His account of co-constructing lessons with students (having them make their own notes, run demos, and track syllabus progress) is offered as a concrete, replicable model of student agency rather than an abstract ideal.

The piece frames sustained follow-through -- always doing what you said you'd do with homework, practicals, and classwork -- as the practical expression of a teacher's sense of mission, not a separate discipline from enjoying the work.
quotes: But with all that said, none of it goes against another deep conviction of mine which is that, in order to sustain a career in teaching, you need to enjoy it, own it and do the things you want to do. Otherwise you just won't stick at it which is no good to anyone.

What I found was that this emerged through them respecting me as a teacher who took them seriously. I'm always super serious and super enthusiastic about achievement, excellence and the ideas in the curriculum.

I think it's true that our UK curriculum is over-stuffed but even here, there are so many choices you can make because, by making them, you yourself are inspired, motivated, reminded of the joy of learning your subject.

I learned that the biggest restriction of student agency is often teachers' lack of confidence that it can work - so you have a vicious circle of teacher doubt leading to a lack of student agency. I reversed that: took some risks, set super high expectations, demanding excellence and the need to meet deadlines and students rose to it time and time again.

That sense of real drive was part of teaching for me. We're not here to muck about and drag ourselves through a murky, drab curriculum - we're here to really think hard, to listen to each other, share ideas, practise hard and wrestle with the hard stuff.

Make teaching the job you want it to be. Teach great lessons - harness all the contemporary wisdom around the science learning; work with colleagues to solve the tricky problems; blend the techniques with your curriculum knowledge and passion your sense of what really matters.
